title: Learning PH/poly from learning NP/poly
formal: Does efficient distribution-free PAC learnability of \(\mathrm{NP/poly}\) from random labeled examples imply the same learnability for every fixed level of \(\mathrm{PH/poly}\)? In the size-parameterized model below, write \(\mathsf{Learn}_r\) for efficient learning of Boolean concepts represented by circuits with \(r\) alternating witness blocks, starting existentially. The target is the single implication \[\mathsf{Learn}_1\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall r\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\ \mathsf{Learn}_r.\] The learner for each fixed \(r\) may be different and have a different polynomial running-time bound. This does not request one polynomial uniform over arbitrarily many alternations. Both sides use ordinary Boolean circuits as output hypotheses and only independent random examples of the unknown target.
why: The question asks whether solving one level of a powerful prediction task automatically solves every fixed level above it. An affirmative answer would give a structural collapse for efficient learning, beyond the familiar collapses for deciding languages or merely representing them by small circuits.

importance.reason: A general structural implication for the polynomial hierarchy in computational learning, with uniform random-example algorithms and nonuniform target classes. It connects complexity-class collapses with a substantially different access model, rather than one isolated concept family.

sentences: The question asks whether efficient PAC learning of NP/poly would imply efficient PAC learning at every fixed level of the polynomial hierarchy.
Targets are small circuits with alternating witness tests, while the learner sees only independent labeled examples from an arbitrary unknown distribution.
The output must be an ordinary efficiently evaluatable Boolean circuit, with polynomial time also accounting for samples, randomness and the public target-size bound.
Known structural equivalences for stronger classes and ordinary circuit-representation collapses do not establish this learning implication.
The full 2021 source explicitly asks the question, while the bounded later-status review supplies no matching resolution and leaves present status uncertain.

definitions:
Fix the ordinary Boolean circuit basis consisting of two-input AND and OR gates, one-input NOT gates, and constants; circuits are acyclic and have one output bit. Fix a standard effective binary encoding. For \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), and fixed \(r\ge1\), let \(\mathcal C_r(n,s)\) contain every function on \(\{0,1\}^n\) of the form \[f(x)=\mathbf1\{\exists u_1\ \forall u_2\ \exists u_3\ \cdots Q_r u_r:\ C(x,u_1,\ldots,u_r)=1\},\] where \(Q_i\) alternates with \(i\), each \(u_i\) ranges over a specified finite Boolean cube, and the total number of input nodes, witness bits and gates of the deterministic matrix circuit \(C\) is at most \(s\). Zero-length witness blocks are allowed. The size is a combinatorial circuit-size bound; encoding such a circuit takes a polynomial number of bits in \(s\). At \(r=1\), these are nondeterministic circuits. Allowing size polynomial in \(n\) gives the usual nonuniform class \(\mathrm{NP/poly}\). The union over every fixed alternation depth gives \(\mathrm{PH/poly}\), the polynomial hierarchy with polynomial-length advice. Equivalently, advice can be included in the matrix circuit; it is not given to the learner. There is no requirement that the target descriptions at different input lengths be produced by one algorithm.

Precisely, \(\mathsf{Learn}_r\) says that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A_r\) and one polynomial \(p_r\) such that the following holds for every \(n,s\) as above, every pair of integers \(a,b\ge3\), every \(f\in\mathcal C_r(n,s)\), and every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Given the public unary parameters \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and independent examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts on every execution in at most \(p_r(n+s+a+b)\) steps and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[\Pr_{A_r,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le 1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer probability includes the random training draws and the machine’s independent fair random bits. The inner probability uses a fresh test draw. Each requested example is an independent draw; requests count toward the time bound and reading its \(n+1\) bits is charged. The bound therefore also limits the number of examples, random bits and output bits. The predictor is evaluated without access to the example source, target or learner state. Its gates have no nondeterministic or higher-hierarchy oracle. It need not use the target’s representation or respect its size bound, but its printed description must fit the learner’s polynomial time.

The learner knows the size bound, not the unknown circuit, its advice, witness assignments, or the distribution. There are no membership queries asking for labels at chosen points, and no equivalence queries. All distributions are admitted; efficient sampling code is not required because the example source is part of the PAC interface. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed concept, so this is realizable rather than agnostic learning. Integer inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters specify the usual arbitrary accuracy and confidence guarantees without numerical-encoding ambiguity. Supplying \(s\) makes explicit the source’s standard polynomial-in-target-size convention: combining all polynomial-size representations at one \(n\) without any size bound would erase the intended computational restriction.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, with a polynomial-time learner for every fixed alternation depth under the hypothesis \(\mathsf{Learn}_1\), or prove its negation \(\mathsf{Learn}_1\land\exists r\ge1,\neg\mathsf{Learn}_r\). All distribution, target-size, accuracy and confidence quantifiers must be preserved. The requested result is a qualitative implication about uniform learning algorithms; it does not ask for a particular optimal exponent. An oracle-relative separation by itself is evidence about relativizing arguments, not a refutation of the unrelativized implication. A theorem about average-case decision algorithms, membership-query learners, or existence of nonuniform hypothesis circuits alone does not establish this random-example learning implication.

source_formulation.text: Does polynomial-time learnability of NP/poly imply polynomial-time learnability of PH/poly?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: An NP/poly concept labels an input by whether some short witness makes a small verification circuit accept. Higher levels alternate existential and universal witness tests. The learner never performs those tests on the hidden target description; it sees only random correctly labeled examples and must produce an efficiently evaluatable prediction circuit.

The classical Karp–Lipton theorem concerns small circuit representations for NP and a resulting collapse of decision complexity. The question here is about finding useful predictors from limited observed data. A guarantee that some small circuit exists is weaker than a learning algorithm that discovers one under every distribution.

Uniformity applies to the learner: for a fixed level, one Turing algorithm must handle every input length, size bound and target circuit. The target class is nonuniform because its hidden descriptions may vary arbitrarily with input length. Neither target advice nor a circuit solving a higher-level decision problem is supplied as free advice to the learner.

The 2021 paper proves stronger equivalences for EXP/poly and PSPACE/poly. In those classes it relates worst-case and average-case learning and shows that restricting the example distribution to uniform or allowing membership queries does not alter the qualitative polynomial-time learnability conclusion. These results concern stronger classes and do not prove the NP-to-PH implication.

The source separately studies restricted reductions from SAT to learning NP/poly. Its hierarchy-collapse consequence for such a reduction concerns a hardness proof with additional structural properties. The existence of that kind of reduction is not part of the premise of this card. The source’s additional question about an oracle-relative obstacle is also separate from the unrelativized implication.

The December 2021 full manuscript explicitly retains the hierarchy question. The January 2025 journal publication is confirmed by the publisher, whose accessible abstract states the paper’s stronger-class and reduction results. Its subscription-only full text was not available in this review. Bounded later-work searches found no checked theorem answering this exact implication, so current status remains qualified rather than certified from publication metadata.
